questions.question: [NEET 2017 | Biology] Down's syndrome is caused by trisomy of chromosome number:
questions.solution: # Answer: **(C) 21** ## Down's Syndrome - Trisomy 21 **Down's syndrome is caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21**, resulting in a total of 47 chromosomes instead of the normal 46 (2n = 47 instead of 2n = 46). --- ## Step-by-Step Understanding: ### Normal Chromosome Pattern: - Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total) - Chromosome 21 normally appears as a pair (two copies) ### In Down's Syndrome: - Instead of 2 copies of chromosome 21, there are **3 copies** - Hence the term **"Trisomy 21"** - Total chromosomes = 47 --- ## Clinical Features of Down's Syndrome: - **Facial features**: Slanted eyes, flat face, protruding tongue - **Intellectual disability**: Variable degree of mental retardation - **Heart defects**: Common cardiac abnormalities - **Low muscle tone**: Hypotonia - **Short stature** --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Chromosome | Condition | Trisomy Name | |-----------|-----------|------------| | 13 | Patau's syndrome | Trisomy 13 | | 18 | Edwards' syndrome | Trisomy 18 | | 21 | **Down's syndrome** | **Trisomy 21** \u₂₇₁₃ | | 23 (X/Y) | Turner's/Klinefelter's syndrome | Sex chromosome abnormality | --- ## Key Fact to Remember: **"Down's syndrome = Trisomy 21"** \— This is one of the most frequently asked questions in NEET. Always associate chromosome 21 with Down's syndrome.

questions.question: [NEET 2021 | Biology] In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa), the phenotypic ratio is:
questions.solution: # Answer: **(B) 3:1** ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: **Setting up the cross:** - Parent 1: Aa (heterozygous) - Parent 2: Aa (heterozygous) **Punnett Square:** | | A | a | |---|----|----| | **A** | AA | Aa | | **a** | Aa | aa | **Offspring genotypes:** - 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa (genotypic ratio = 1:2:1) **Phenotypic classification:** - **AA** → Dominant phenotype ✓ - **Aa** → Dominant phenotype ✓ (heterozygotes show dominant trait) - **aa** → Recessive phenotype ✗ **Phenotypic ratio = 3:1** - 3 individuals with dominant phenotype - 1 individual with recessive phenotype ## Key Concept: This **3:1 ratio** is Mendel's classic monohybrid cross result. The dominant allele masks the recessive allele in heterozygotes, so both AA and Aa individuals appear identical phenotypically. ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: - **(A) 1:2:1** → This is the **genotypic ratio**, not phenotypic - **(C) 1:1** → This occurs in a **testcross** (Aa × aa), not heterozygote × heterozygote - **(D) 9:3:3:1** → This is a **dihybrid cross** ratio (two traits) **Remember:** In monohybrid crosses between heterozygotes, you'll always get a **3:1 phenotypic ratio**! 📊

questions.question: In Drosophila melanogaster , what percentage of recombination is shown between the genes white and yellow, and what percentage of linkage is shown between the genes white and miniature wing, respectively?
questions.solution: **Correct Answer: (A)** **Explanation:** In Drosophila melanogaster, genes for white and yellow colour are about 1.3 map unit distant from each other so they show 1.3 % recombinations while 98.7% linkage (or parental characters). Genes for white colour and miniature wing are about 37.2 map unit distant so they show 37.2% recombinations and 62.8% linkage (or parental characters). **Key Point:** Always read all options carefully and eliminate wrong ones using fundamental NCERT concepts.

questions.question: The figure shows the experiment of T.H. Morgan on the linkage. If in cross-I, genes are tightly linked and in cross-II, genes are loosely linked then what will be the percentage of recombination produced in cross-I and cross-II respectively?
questions.solution: **Correct Answer: (A)** **Explanation:** Morgan and his students have found that linked genes show varied recombinations, some being more tightly linked than others, (i) In Drosophila, the crossing of yellow bodied (y) and white-eyed (w) female with brown bodied (y + ) red-eyed (w + ) male-produced F₁ to be brown bodied and red-eyed females, while males were yellow bodied and white eyed. On intercrossing of F₁ progeny, Morgan observed that the two genes did not segregate independently of each other and, therefore, the F₂ ratio deviated significantly from expected 9: 3: 3: 1 ratio. He found that 98.7% to be of the parental type and only 1.3% recombinant type. (ii) In a second cross of Drosophila between white-eyed and miniature winged (wwmm) female with wild type or red-eyed normal winged (w + m + ) males, all the F₁ were found to be of wild type, i.e., red-eyed and normal winged in females, while it was white-eyed and miniature wings in males. An F₁ female fly was then test crossed with white-eyed and miniature winged male. 62.8% of the progeny was of parental types while 37.2% were recombinant types. **Key Point:** Always read all options carefully and eliminate wrong ones using fundamental NCERT concepts.

questions.question: [NEET 2020 | Biology] Cross TT x tt -> all tall F₁. F₁ x tt gives:
questions.solution: # Answer: **(A) 50% tall 50% short** --- ## Step-by-Step Solution ### Step 1: Identify the F₁ Genotype **Cross: TT × tt → F₁** Since all F₁ are tall, and we're crossing a homozygous dominant (TT) with homozygous recessive (tt): - **F₁ genotype = Tt** (heterozygous) - **F₁ phenotype = Tall** (T is dominant) ### Step 2: Perform the Test Cross **F₁ × tt = Tt × tt** This is called a **test cross** (crossing heterozygote with homozygous recessive). ### Step 3: Use Punnett Square | | **t** | **t** | |---|---|---| | **T** | Tt | Tt | | **t** | tt | tt | ### Results: - **50% Tt** (tall - because T is dominant) - **50% tt** (short - homozygous recessive) --- ## Key Concept to Remember **Test Cross Ratio Rule:** > When you cross a **heterozygote (Aa) with a homozygous recessive (aa)**, you always get a **1:1 phenotypic ratio** (50:50) This is because: - Heterozygote produces 50% A and 50% a gametes - Homozygous recessive only produces a gametes - Result: 50% Aa (dominant phenotype) and 50% aa (recessive phenotype) --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong | Option | Why It's Wrong | |--------|---| | (B) All tall | Would need both parents to be TT or F₁ to be homozygous | | (C) All short | Would require T allele to be absent | | (D) 75% tall 25% short | This is F₂ ratio (Tt × Tt), not a test cross result |

questions.question: [NEET 2020 | Biology] Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disease. A carrier female marries a normal male. What percentage of sons will have haemophilia?
questions.solution: # Answer: **(C) 50%** --- ## Step-by-Step Solution: ### Genetic Setup: - **Carrier female**: X^HX^h (heterozygous - one normal, one haemophilia allele) - **Normal male**: X^HY (normal allele on X chromosome) ### Punnett Square: | | X^H (from father) | Y (from father) | |---|---|---| | **X^H (from mother)** | X^HX^H (normal daughter) | X^HY (normal son) | | **X^h (from mother)** | X^HX^h (carrier daughter) | **X^h Y (haemophiliac son)** | ### Results: - **All daughters**: Normal or carriers (0% affected) - **Sons**: - 50% X^HY (normal) - **50% X^h Y (haemophiliac)** \u₂₇₁₃ --- ## Key Concept: **Sex-linked recessive inheritance pattern:** - Males need only ONE recessive allele to express the disease (hemizygous condition) - Females need TWO recessive alleles to be affected - Carrier mothers pass the recessive allele to 50% of offspring - Of those offspring who receive it, ALL sons will be affected (no second X to mask it) --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: - **(A) 0%** - Would be true if the mother was homozygous normal (X^HX^H) - **(B) 25%** - This would occur if both parents were carriers or affected - **(D) 100%** - Would require the father to be haemophiliac (X^h Y) --- ## Remember: For X-linked recessive disorders, carrier females (X^HX^h) always have a **50% chance** of passing the recessive allele to each child, and **all sons inheriting it will be affected**.
